content.title: Official Blind Review #2
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I carefully checked the derivations and theory.
content.review:
Adversarial neural pruning

This paper proposes “adversarial neural pruning” method and vulnerability suppression loss to defend against adversarial attacks. For adversarial neural pruning, the authors train a pruning mask in an adversarial way that benefits both the clean accuracy and the adversarial robustness. The authors also propose a new loss function “vulnerability loss” that measures the robustness of intermediate features in neural networks. By using both techniques, the authors demonstrate through experiments that it is an effective method to defend against adversarial attacks.

I have the following questions:
Q1: Don’t understand definition 1 and definition 2?
I don’t quite understand the meaning of definition 1 and 2. It seems useless for the presentation of the paper to me. Can the authors illustrate why you define these two notions here? Is there any usage in this paper for defining (\epsilon, \delta)-robust and (\epsilon, \delta)-vulnerable?
Q2: How do you compute the vulnerability of a network?
The authors define the vulnerability of a feature in equation (1). However, I can not find how such vulnerability measure is computed exactly. Can the authors specify how they compute this  vulnerability measure?
Q3: In page 4 “We emphasize that our proposed method can be extended to any existing or new sparsification method in a similar way”
This claim is not carefully discussed in this paper. Can your approach be applied to [1]? 
Q4: Title does not properly cover the content of this paper?
The author proposed two approaches: adversarial neural pruning and vulnerability loss. However, the title seems to only cover one of them. It is misleading since vulnerability loss seems also to be a major part of the proposed method. Therefore, either the title needs to be changed or the structure of this paper should be altered to highlight adversarial neural pruning approach.

[1] Learning both Weights and Connections for Efficient Neural Networks. Song Han, Jeff Pool, John Tran, William J. Dally, NIPS 2015.

content.title: Response to review 2
content.comment:
Thank you for your reviews. Please allow us to address your questions here.

Q1: Don’t understand definition 1 and definition 2? I don’t quite understand the meaning of definition 1 and 2. It seems useless for the presentation of the paper to me. Can the authors illustrate why you define these two notions here? Is there any usage in this paper for defining (\epsilon, \delta)-robust and (\epsilon, \delta)-vulnerable?

Answer: These definitions are essential for the paper as to our knowledge we are the first to formally describe the robustness and vulnerability of a latent feature which is necessarily required to explain the vulnerability of a network later in our paper. We also show the demonstration of a robust and vulnerable feature in the appendix in Figure D.1 based on these definitions.

Q2: How do you compute the vulnerability of a network? The authors define the vulnerability of a feature in equation (1). However, I can not find how such a vulnerability measure is computed exactly. Can the authors specify how they compute this vulnerability measure?

Answer: For measuring the vulnerability of a feature, we simply compute the absolute difference of that feature value for a clean and adversarial example to measure the amount of distortion in that feature value in the presence of an adversary. We then compute the expectation overall all the features and examples to obtain the vulnerability of the network.

Q3: In page 4 “We emphasize that our proposed method can be extended to any existing or new sparsification method in a similar way” This claim is not carefully discussed in this paper. Can your approach be applied to [1]?

Answer: We would like to clarify: “We emphasize that our proposed method can be extended to any existing or new *bayesian* sparsification method in a similar way”. Since our method learns a Bayesian dropout mask and is not just based on pruning based on heuristics criterions like the magnitude of weights or activations as in the Han et al. [1] so ANP cannot be applied to it but vulnerability suppression as a regularizer can be directly used. We have further shown the results for an additional sparsification method based on Variational Information Bottleneck [2] in the appendix of our paper.

[1] Learning both Weights and Connections for Efficient Neural Networks. Song Han, Jeff Pool, John Tran, William J. Dally, NIPS 2015.
[2] Compressing Neural Networks using the Variational Information Bottleneck, ICML 18

content.title: Official Blind Review #3
content.review_assessment:_checking_correctness_: I assessed the sensibility of the derivations and theory.
content.review:
This paper proposed an adversarial training method that aims to obtaining sparse and robust networks at the same time. First, the vulnerability is defined at the latent feature space and measured as the expected difference between clean latent feature vectors and adversarial latent feature vectors across all layers. Then this vulnerability measure is incorporated as a regularization and the network is trained in an adversarial training setting. A Bayesian sparsification algorithm is used to prune the network at the same time. The method makes sense to me. However, my main concern is the evaluation. See below for more details.

It seems no other defense algorithm except AT has been compared with ANP and its variants. Since this paper, to my understanding, is an adversarial defense algorithm, it should be compared to other SOTA defense algorithms.

How does this method work for different adversarial attacks? ANP is trained under L_inf black and white box attacks (Papernot et al., 2016), and test under the same attacks. What if trained attacks are different to the attacks at the test time. Will the robustness is generalizable across different attacks?

The 3rd loss in Eq.6: why is the mask only optimized on the loss on the adversarial examples? Why not with the clean example loss?

Eq. 1: is that an L1 or L2 norm?

Definitions 1 and 2 are almost identical with only 1 or 2 different words. Can you combine them to make it more concise?

In summary, without the thorough evaluations as suggested above, it’s hard to see if the proposed method is competitive or not.

content.title: Response to reviewer 3
content.comment:
Thank you for your reviews and insights. Please allow us to address your comments here:

****Comment 1: It seems no other defense algorithm except AT has been compared with ANP and its variants. Since this paper, to my understanding, is an adversarial defense algorithm, it should be compared to other SOTA defense algorithms.

====Answer: We strongly disagree that we lack comparison to state-of-the-art defense methods. We would like to bring this to the notice of reviewer that we don’t just compare with Adversarial training (AT) but also Pretrained Adversarial Training (Pre-trained AT) [1], Adversarial Bayesian Neural Network (AT BNN) [2] (See Table 3), our method largely outperforms both these methods in terms of clean accuracy, adversarial accuracy and vulnerability of the network. We would also like to highlight that our method can be applied on any existing or new defense method as it only requires the addition of regularized loss or a dropout mask on the top of the defense which shows the versatility of our proposed framework.

****Comment 2: How does this method work for different adversarial attacks? ANP is trained under L_inf black and white box attacks (Papernot et al., 2016), and test under the same attacks. What if trained attacks are different from the attacks at the test time. Will the robustness is generalizable across different attacks?

====Answer: We agree that generalization across different attacks is a compelling direction, but we feel that it is outside of the scope of this particular work. It has been shown that most of the existing defenses do not generalize across multiple attacks [3][4]. In this paper we focus on building intuition and exploring the underlying methodology, providing comprehensive experiments to back up our claims. We use the attack parameters and settings as used in all the existing state-of-the-art baselines and our method can be extended to any other attack correspondingly.

****Comment 3: The 3rd loss in Eq.6: why is the mask only optimized on the loss of the adversarial examples? Why not with the clean example loss?

====Answer: The mask is optimized to keep the robust features i.e the features which are important for adversarial robustness. Our choice is intuitive and straightforward as if it is optimized on both the adversarial examples and clean examples it might lead to the addition of some vulnerable features to increase generalization which can hurt the model’s robustness.

****Comment 4: Eq. 1: is that an L1 or L2 norm?

====Answer: Equation 1 is the L1 norm of the difference between the value of the feature in the presence of a clean example and value of the feature in the presence of an adversarial example.

[1] Using Pre Training Can Improve Model Robustness and Uncertainity, ICML 19
[2] Adv-BNN: Improved Adversarial Defense through Robust Bayesian Neural Network, ICLR 19
[3] Towards the first adversarially robust neural network model on MNIST, ICLR 19
[4] Adversarial Training and Robustness for Multiple Perturbations, Neurips 19

content.review:
This paper presents an approach to improve DNN robustness to adversarial attacks. The main novelty relies on defining vulnerability in the latent feature space. The algorithm trains with an additional term to promote similar features between an input and its adversarial counterpart.

I like the paper and the idea behind. Here are some comments that would be nice to address.
Method:
- Efficiency-wise, how is this implemented?  If I understand correctly, the training process is less efficient as the features need to be stored and compared, right?
- Any guarantees to make sure the vulnerability does not reduce the capacity of the model?

- I like the idea of moving the robustness to hidden layers. The paper proposes a metric (the regularizer) to get features closer. While that sounds interesting (I assume resulting features would be agnostic to the input), the evaluation shows that the metric does not correlate with the robustness. 
- I would rephrase all around the objectives for training the model J(\theta...). 
- I find difficult to follow around Eq. 7
Experiments:

- The way it is written, is very confusing: ANP leads to 88% reduction in memory while maintaining similar robustness... what about clean accuracy? If clean accuracy is not valid, the entire system is irrelevant.
- I am not sure how to read the numbers. I can understand some measures are relevant (accuracy to attacks) but at the expense of a huge clean accuracy drop (69% to 57%). I rather would tune the proposal to achieve similar accuracy and then be able to compare just the robustness. 
- In the experimental section, I am missing the size of the resulting network. As there are neurons set to zero, that value is relevant. 
- The contribution of VS seems relevant over AT but marginal on ANP. Please, elaborate. 
- Lack of correlation between vulnerability and robustness in the experiments. Please, elaborate. 


Other comments:

- I think the overall organization needs improvement. The experimental section has plenty of numbers repeated in different tables and that consumes space and is confusing.

content.title: Response to reviewer 1
content.comment:
We gratefully thank the reviewer for the detailed and valuable comments and notes. Please allow us to address them here.

****Comment 1: Efficiency-wise, how is this implemented? If I understand correctly, the training process is less efficient as the features need to be stored and compared, right?

====Answer: This seems to be a misunderstanding. Adversarial neural pruning or our proposed vulnerability suppression regularizer has no overhead compared to the default adversarial training and pruning procedures. For ANP, we don’t need to store the features as it simply involves the standard Bayesian optimization for the pruning mask over the adversarial examples and for the vulnerability suppression, we do the comparison on the fly for every iteration which makes our learning framework highly efficient and robust.

****Comment 2: I like the idea of moving the robustness to hidden layers. The paper proposes a metric (the regularizer) to get features closer. While that sounds interesting (I assume resulting features would be agnostic to the input), the evaluation shows that the metric does not correlate with the robustness
**** Comment 3: Lack of correlation between vulnerability and robustness in the experiments. Please, elaborate.

====Answer: We thank the reviewer for pointing this out. We indeed observed that vulnerability metric is not correlated with robustness in terms of adversarial accuracy which highlights the susceptibility of all the existing adversarial defenses which improve the robustness only at the input space. Our proposed method provides robustness at both the input and latent feature space which we feel will open the doors for research to understand the behaviour of latent-features robustness and lead to a much more practical and effective defense.

****Comment 4: I find difficult to follow around Eq. 7

====Answer: Please refer to our proof for equation 7 in the appendix for a detailed explanation.

****Comment 5: The way it is written, is very confusing: ANP leads to 88% reduction in memory while maintaining similar robustness... what about clean accuracy? If clean accuracy is not valid, the entire system is irrelevant. - I am not sure how to read the numbers. I can understand some measures are relevant (accuracy to attacks) but at the expense of a huge clean accuracy drop (69% to 57%). I rather would tune the proposal to achieve similar accuracy and then be able to compare just the robustness.

====Answer: It has been well known in the literature that adversarial robustness leads to a loss in clean accuracy [1][2]. We would like to highlight here that the loss in clean accuracy is not due to our proposed method and it is an aftereffect of adversarial training. We would also like to emphasize that our method outperforms all the existing state-of-the-art defense mechanisms in terms of clean accuracy which is due to the fact that sparsification helps to regularize models. 

****Comment 6: In the experimental section, I am missing the size of the resulting network. As there are neurons set to zero, that value is relevant.

====Answer: We have provided the details of the computational efficiency of the networks across various metrics including the FLOPs, Memory and sparsity percentage in the appendix due to space constraints, please refer to Table Appendix-1 in the appendix. We will further update our paper with all the computation results in the next revision.

****Comment 7: The contribution of VS seems relevant over AT but marginal on ANP. Please, elaborate.

====Answer: We thank the reviewer for highlighting this out since Adversarial training (AT) aims for robustness only at the input space, the latent features are still vulnerable as an outcome of which contribution of VS seems relevant over AT as it suppresses the vulnerability at the latent space by ~50% and shows significant improvement. However, ANP already suppresses the vulnerability at the latent space by ~50% which makes the effect of VS marginal on ANP.

[1] Robustness May Be at Odds with Accuracy, ICLR 18
[2] Theoretically Principled Trade-off between Robustness and Accuracy, ICML 19
